newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Harney aims to be first Irish woman govt leader.
newsitem.headline: Harney aims to be first Irish woman govt leader.

text.p: As head of the small, right-wing Progressive Democrat Party, Mary Harney, hopes to be the first woman to lead a political party into government in Ireland after Friday's election.
Admired by many voters for her honesty and outspokenness, Harney, 44, hopes to form the next government with Fianna Fail, the party she split from in 1985.

Political sources say she is demanding a top job in cabinet in return for backing such a coalition and could well be Ireland's next foreign or finance minister, the first woman to hold either post, as well as deputy prime minister.
A mould-breaker, Harney's political career began 20 years ago when she was nominated to the Irish Senate, the upper house of parliament, as its youngest ever member.
She was elected to the Dail, or lower house, for Fianna Fail in 1981 but broke with that party four years later to become a founding member of the Progressive Democrats.

The establishment of the new party, and its 1989 decision to form a coalition with Fianna Fail, are widely credited with breaking the mould in which Irish politics had been mired since the civil war of the 1920s.
In that 1989 coalition government, Harney became a junior minister at the Environment Ministry where her greatest achievement was solving Dublin's smog problem by banning the use of smoky coal.
Regarded as one of the best speakers in the Irish parliament, Harney's politics have been described as instinctive and populist rather than ideological.
Her pronouncements on issues such as standards in public life have struck a chord with many voters and her personal popularity rating with the electorate has remained consistently high.
"Her political judgement is sometimes faulty, frequently short-term but she possesses a journalist's eye for the right question and the good headline," one political commentator has said of her.

What position she can expect in government will depend largely on the performance of the Progressive Democrats in Friday's election when the party hopes to increase its representation in the 166-seat parliament to 15 from eight.
Fiscally conservative, the Progressive Democrats are committed to cutting taxes, controlling spending and clamping down on crime if they are elected.
In their manifesto, they promise to reduce the present basic rate of tax to 20 percent from 26 percent and to cut the higher rate to 40 percent from 48 percent.

The Progressive Democrats also distinguish themselves from other political parties with their firm belief in privatisation, promising to use the proceeds from the sale of state companies to reduce Ireland's national debt.
"In the modern world, there is no rationale for state involvement in the running of hotels, fertiliser factories and other commercial enterprises," Harney has said.
They take a different tack on European economic and monetary union (EMU) as well, expressing reservations about Ireland joining a single currency without Britain.
On this, Harney is at odds with her prospective coalition partners, Fianna Fail, who are committed to joining the single currency in the first wave, with or without sterling.
This, and other differences, have led to accusations that their proposed partnership is merely "a coalition of convenience".

But Harney says a Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government would be based on trust between its two leaders who have known each other for 20 years and are seen as belonging to a younger generation of Irish politicians.
